title: Travelling on Light

paragraphs.text: In the same way as sailors have navigated the oceans of the Earth for thousands of years using the force of the wind, so astronauts dream of navigating the universe by using light to propel them. Sailing on light is the only technology that can someday take us to the stars.' says Louis Friedman, director of the Planetary Society. a worldwide organisation of space enthusiasts. Friedman announced recently that the society, with financial help from an anonymous donor, would be taking the first steps on a journey which sounds like science fiction, but which may one day be feasible. Over the next few years, the society will build and fly a series of solar-sail spacecraft named ‘LightSails’, first in orbit around the Earth and eventually into deeper space.

The solar sail receives its driving force from the simple fact that light carries not just energy but also momentum — a fact proved by comet tails. which consist of dust blown by sunlight from a comet's core. The force on a solar sail is gentle, if not feeble, but unlike a rocket, which fires for a few minutes at most it is constant. Over days and years a big enough sail, for example about a mile across, could reach speeds of hundreds of thousands of miles an hour, fast enough to traverse the solar system in five years. Riding the beam from a powerful laser, a sail could even make the journey to another star system in 100 years, that is to say, the age-span of a human.

Whether humans could make such trips one day remains doubtful, although the technology needed to make trial trips might be developed at some point. Friedman says it would be too risky and involve too much exposure to radiation to sail humans to a place such as Mars. He says the only passengers on an interstellar voyage — even after 200 years of additional technological development — are likely to be small robots, or perhaps our genomes encoded on a computer chip, a consequence of the need to keep the craft light, like a giant cosmic kite.

In principle, a solar sail can do anything a normal sail can do, like tacking backwards and forwards. Unlike other spacecraft, it can act as an antigravity machine, using solar pressure to balance the sun's gravity and thus hover in space. And of course, it does not have to carry rocket fuel. ‘Think centuries or millennia, not decades,’ says Freeman Dyson of the Institute of Advanced Study in the US of any trip powered by a space sail. ‘We ought to be doing things which are romantic’, he says, adding that nobody knows yet how to build sails big and thin enough for serious travel. ‘You have to get equipment for unrolling and stretching them — a big piece of engineering that's not been done. But the joy of technology is that it's unpredictable’. Many of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's (NASA) laboratories have studied solar sails. Scientists from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory even investigated sending a solar sail to encounter and ride along with Halley's Comet during its pass in 1986. But NASA's efforts have ceased as it searches for dollars to keep the human space-flight programme going, says Donna Shirley, a retired engineer and former chairwoman of the NASA Institute for Advanced Concepts. Shirley says that the solar sail is feasible and that the only issue is financial.

Japan continues to have a programme, and trial solar sails have been deployed from satellites and rockets, but no one as yet has tried to sail them anywhere. An effort by the Planetary Society and the Russian Academy of Sciences to launch a sail about 100 feet wide, known as Cosmos-1, from a Russian missile submarine ended with the sail at the bottom of the sea.

Friedman was looking for money for a Cosmos-2 when NASA asked if the society wanted to take over a smaller project, called the Nanosail. Nanosails are only 18 feet wide and are designed to increase atmospheric drag and thus help satellites out of orbit. Friedman accepted, and adapted the Nanosail into the LightSail, which is made of aluminised plastic film about a quarter of the thickness of a rubbish bag. The body of the spacecraft will consist of three miniature satellites known as CubeSats which were first developed by students at Stanford University in the US. One of the cubes will hold electronics and the other two will carry folded-up sails. Assembled like blocks, the whole thing looks like a box the same size as a loaf of bread, and weighs less than 11 pounds.

The LightSail missions will be spread about 12 months apart with the timing depending on what rockets are available to give LightSail a ride. Friedman says the first flight. LightSail-1, will be judged a success if the sail can be controlled for even a small part of an orbit, and shows any sign of being accelerated by sunlight The next flight will feature a larger sail and will last several days, building up enough velocity to raise its orbit by tens or hundreds of miles. For the third flight. Friedman and his colleagues intend to send LightSail out of the Earth's orbit with a package of scientific instruments to monitor the output of the sun and provide early warning of magnetic storms, which can disrupt power grids and even damage spacecraft.
